claims.text: NbTaTiZrV0.5 exhibits a high-temperature hardness plateau.
The plateau in NbTaTiZrV0.5 occurs approximately between 673 K and 1073 K.
The plateau arises because edge dislocations undergo thermally activated super-jogging.
Thermally activated super-jogging increases the pinning effectiveness of edge dislocations.
Increasing temperature supplies edge dislocations with sufficient thermal energy to activate super-jogging.
Super-jogging creates localized pinning points on edge dislocations.
Enhanced pinning slows dislocation motion and counterbalances ordinary thermal softening.
The balance between enhanced pinning and thermal softening produces a plateau in yield strength.
The initial NbTaTiZrV0.5 material is well annealed, single phase, microstructurally uniform, and contains minimal secondary phases.
Temperature-dependent mechanical testing and in-situ TEM can be used to track strength and dislocation dynamics from room temperature to 1073 K.
Between 673 K and 1073 K, the yield strength of NbTaTiZrV0.5 will undergo minimal reduction.
Pinned edge dislocations will be denser or more active in the plateau region than outside that region.
Pinned edge dislocations will be denser or more active in NbTaTiZrV0.5 than in a screw-dislocation-dominated control alloy.
Typical BCC metals and other HEAs are dominated by screw dislocations and lack good high-temperature strength.
A screw-dislocation-controlled comparison alloy should soften monotonically with temperature and exhibit no plateau.
The proposed mechanism applies only while phase stability and microstructural uniformity are maintained and significant secondary-phase formation or competing deformation mechanisms are absent.
Short-range ordering, dynamic phase transformations, or nanotwinning can limit the applicability of the super-jogging mechanism when they dominate deformation.
Failure to observe either the specified yield-strength plateau or increased pinned-edge-dislocation activity would falsify the hypothesis.
